title: Joel Roberts Poinsett → James Monroe, Santiago de Chile, despatch with at least nine cipher passages printed as '(undeciphered cipher)'
correspondents: Joel Roberts Poinsett (US special agent and consul general for Buenos Aires, Chile and Peru) → James Monroe, Secretary of State
shelfmark: NARA RG 59, Despatches from Special Agents, vol. 3 (Poinsett 1813-23) = microfilm M37 roll 2, catalog naId 213803757; Poinsett's other 1811-14 reports ('parts in cipher') are in the Poinsett Papers vol. 4, Historical Society of Pennsylvania (Gilpin collection)
folio_note: nine '(undeciphered cipher)' insertions in Manning's text, single words to whole clauses (on the Carreras, the Buenos Aires army, the Portuguese, the Araucanian chief); frame of the letter not located (M37 roll 2 frames 16-24 are the Poinsett list and his 'State of society' essay) Frame located 27 Oct 2026 (research/nara_triage_a/): M37 roll 2, frame 0093; a coded sibling of 14 June 1814 is at frames 0097-0099.
status: Manning 1925 vol. 2, doc. 442, pp. 896-897, prints the despatch with '(undeciphered cipher)' at each coded passage; the State Department returned Poinsett's other letters to him in 1818, so his own copies (some 'Part in cipher', May-July 1811 from Buenos Aires, per the HSP list filmed at M37 roll 2 frames 20-22) are at HSP, possibly with plaintext drafts. Not in the repo (known.py: Poinsett no hits). Worked 28 Oct 2026 (targets/poinsett1813, write-up poinsett1813): 437 groups transcribed; the same-code letter of 14 June 1814 (no. 651) carries a clerk's decipherment, 95 values, 161 of 437 groups of 1813 get a value, no sentence reads. Other State Department rolls searched (M37 1-2, M70, M77, M84): no further letter in the code.
why: Poinsett was an active partisan of the Carreras in the first Chilean republic; the hidden passages are his own views on the Chilean leadership and the war with Peru, otherwise unrecorded in US files.
source: NARA RG 59 diplomatic despatches (via Manning 1925) sweep

title: José Rafael Revenga → Colombian Secretary of Foreign Affairs, Madrid, letter partly in cipher intercepted by the French, sent to Washington by Anderson with no key
correspondents: José Rafael Revenga (Colombian envoy in Spain) → Pedro Gual, Secretary of Foreign Affairs of Colombia (paper enclosed by Richard C. Anderson, US minister at Bogotá → John Quincy Adams)
date: 1822 (duplicate intercepted in France; delivered at Bogotá, transmitted 19 Jan 1824)
shelfmark: NARA RG 59, Despatches from US Ministers to Colombia, vol. 3, enclosure 'No. 4' (paper in fragments) to Anderson's despatch of 19 Jan 1824 (microfilm T33)
folio_note: a paper in fragments, written partly in cipher; Manning: 'Not printed. A postscript to Anderson's letter explains that no key to the cipher was furnished. The portions not in cipher are, alone, unintelligible.'
status: Manning 1925 vol. 2, doc. 641, pp. 1272-73. Gual told Anderson it was the duplicate of a Revenga letter from Madrid sent through France, intercepted and opened there, then handed by Count Landos (a French agent at Cartagena, 1822) to a Colombian agent. Revenga's other cipher letters (Archivo General de la Nación, Bogotá; Archivo Santander) may share the key. Not in the repo (known.py: Revenga no hits). 27 Oct 2026 (WAINUT, PR #109; targets/revenga1822/, in progress): key recovered from the ciphertext alone; deciphered in part on a first-pass transcription of the four frames.
why: Colombia's first envoy to Spain reporting on the 1822 negotiations for recognition, a letter the French secret service read and the Colombians passed to the US to warn of French designs.
source: NARA RG 59 diplomatic despatches (via Manning 1925) sweep

title: Hindu–German conspiracy cipher material: Heramba Lal Gupta's cipher letter, the Chakravarty cipher message, and a telegram 'not as yet satisfactorily deciphered'
correspondents: Heramba Lal Gupta / Chandra Kanta Chakravarty and the Indian committee -> German agents
shelfmark: NARA RG 165, MID files 10020-87, 9771-23 (M1194 roll 91, frame 0195); RG 65 OG 1396 (M1085 card); M1085 roll 760 frame 0286 (printed account)
folio_note: Gupta letter: one cipher letter (card only). Telegram: given only in substance in a printed account filed in the BI case.
status: The M1194 card (10020-87, 7 Nov 1917) lists Gupta's cipher letter with no solution. M1085 roll 760 frame 0286 carries a printed account of the case that quotes the telegram's substance and says it 'has not been as yet satisfactorily deciphered'. MI-8 (Manly) read other Hindu-conspiracy letters (Ghose, 10531-409), so the system family is known. Update 28 Oct 2026 (NARA Chicago sweep): the Chicago trial (Crim. 6082) is digitised (Bill of Exceptions naId 540798683, pp. 157-158): Friedman testifies that Government's Exhibit 'Code', a Gupta letter to Albourge at Territet (16 Nov 1916 per the sweep), was decoded at Riverbank and the decipherment is read into the record, so that letter was read at the time. Whether MID card 10020-87 is the same letter is unchecked; the Chakravarty message and the telegram remain open.
why: Cipher evidence from the San Francisco Hindu–German conspiracy trial of 1917-18.
source: NARA bulk-scan triage (slice E, RG 165/RG 65 cipher-word pass)

title: Soviet and German cipher radiograms of 1921 (Moscow ↔ Berlin, Stockholm, Christiania, Kharkov), intercepted at Constantinople by the US High Commission and never deciphered
correspondents: Chicherin / Narkomindel Moscow ↔ Soviet representation Berlin (Kopp, Krestinsky, 'Polpred'), Stockholm, Christiania, Reval; Nikolaev → Kharkov; Auswärtiges Amt Berlin ↔ Deutsche Vertretung Moskau (Hilger); copies sent by Admiral Mark L. Bristol, US High Commissioner, Constantinople
shelfmark: NARA RG 59, Central Decimal File 1910-29, 861.00 (Political Affairs, Russia), microfilm M316 rolls 40-48 (RG 64 digital copies): file units naId 604700562 (861.00/8376-8492, Mar 1921), 604701877 (8493-8622, Apr), 604703234 (8623-8773, May-Jun), 604704577 (8774-8910, Jun-Jul), 604705830 (8911-9012, Jul-Sep), 604707113 (9013-9064, Sep-Oct), 604708415 (9065-9159, Oct-Nov), 604709981 (9160-9240, Nov-Dec), 604711297 (9241-9329, Dec 1921-Feb 1922); the War Department copies are RG 457, Archival and Historian's Source Files, 6707N 'Russian Coded Messages, 1921 (Provided by U.S. High Commissioner Constantinople)' (naId 23890165, not digitised)
folio_note: Typed copies of intercepted radiograms, one per frame with date, route and addresses (e.g. 'MARCH 22d 1921 FROM ... TO MOSCOW 71915 67404 33684 ...'; 'SEPTEMBER 4th 1921 FROM BERLIN TO MOSCOW SCHITSCHERIN MOSKAU FUNKSPRUCH'; 'SEPTEMBER 28th 1921 FROM MOSCOW TO BERLIN POLPRED BERLIN'), mostly 4- and 5-figure groups. Frames with cipher text by roll (OCR count): M316-040 0889-0893 (5); 041 0543-1068 (61); 042 0244-1276 (83); 043 0427-1204 (42); 044 0186-1073 (56); 045 0048-0638 (22); 046 0178-1178 (45); 047 0155-1070 (64); 048 0128-0766 (13): about 390 frames, about 62,000 groups. Covering despatches: 861.00/8575 (Bristol No. 153, 20 Apr 1921, M316-041-0871: the Russian intercept operator's notes on the traffic), 040-0888 (March 1921: hopes anti-Bolshevik Russians may help find the key; Col. Castle sending similar messages to the War Department), 043-0936 (July 1921: 'unable to report any progress regarding the deciphering of the code messages of the Bolshevik Government'); 9071, 9130, 9132, 9133 (Oct-Nov 1921, Moscow-Berlin and Moscow-Christiania). M316-041-1073 'Deciphered telegrams of Soviet authorities' (Petrograd-Reval) is a separate, small set in clear.

links.label: Bristol No. 153 with the operator's notes (M316-041-0871)

status: Unblocked 27 Oct 2026 (NARA slice L, research/nara_triage_l/): the purport list (naId 87657409) led to the 861.00 file, which is filmed on M316 and digitised as RG 64 copies; all nine 1921 rolls fetched and the OCR read. The High Commission could not decipher the traffic and the Department records no decipherment; the War Department (MI-8) received parallel copies (RG 457 6707N). Some of the same Soviet traffic may have been read by GC&CS (HW 12, 1921) and the German side is Auswärtiges Amt traffic; neither has been checked. Distinct from 710 (Chicherin → Sukhanov 1918).
why: A large, dated corpus of early Soviet and German diplomatic cipher radio traffic from 1921, filed as typed copies with the intercept operator's notes: the Rapallo-era Moscow-Berlin channel, unread by the Americans who collected it.
language: Russian and German (per the intercept operator: Kopp–Chicherin traffic mostly Russian, some Chicherin telegrams German)

title: Communist Party of America underground: book-cipher addresses and names in letters seized at 170 Bleecker St., New York, 1920-21
correspondents: District organizers and members (signing D.O. 5, J. Mortin, Frederick Mayer ...) ↔ the Executive Secretary ("EXSEC", Paul Holt), Communist Party of America
shelfmark: NARA RG 65, Investigative Case Files of the Bureau of Investigation 1908-1922, Old German Files (M1085) roll 940, case 202600 ("202600-1775 THRU 202600-1949-1 (4 of 4)", naId 369272950), multi-page PDFs M1085-940A, -940B, -940C ("Copies of Letters & Documents Found at 170 Bleecker St.")
folio_note: OCR count: 77 runs of line/letter fraction groups (e.g. "(New code) 3/3 3/4 2/8 3/7 1/14 - 7/3 2/7 4/4 ...", "Old code P 14 ... 14/15 2/1 6/4"), about 2,400 fraction tokens over the three PDFs. 27 runs are followed by a Bureau "Decode:" or "the above code reads as follows" line; about 50 runs show no decode nearby. 940C also copies the party's own instruction for the system (count lines down, letters across on a set page; a dash between words).
status: Seen in the OCR of the digitised reel: Bureau agents copied the seized letters and decoded many of the coded addresses (class A: decodes in the same file give cribs for the page). The undecoded runs are names, addresses and telegraph covers. Not on DECODE; nothing in the repo. 27 Oct 2026 (WAINUT, PR #116; targets/cpa1920/, in progress): 28 runs and 439 tokens on the typed pages (the 77 runs / 2,400 tokens of the OCR count also took in dates and ratios); handwritten pages not yet searched. Key grid rebuilt from the Bureau's own decodes of 16 runs; the book is not identified.
why: The early US Communist underground (after the Palmer raids) hid its contact network in a book code; the undecoded runs would name more of that network, and the system is a clean example of a period book cipher.

title: British consular cipher telegrams (Vigo → Foreign Office 1939; Gibraltar ↔ British consul Las Palmas, Lisbon/Lagos → consul Tenerife 1940), copies obtained by the German naval attaché Madrid and sent to OKW/Chi
correspondents: British consul Vigo → Foreign Office London; British authorities Gibraltar, Lisbon, Lagos → British consuls Las Palmas and Tenerife
shelfmark: NARA RG 242, T1022 (Copies of Records of the German Navy), rolls 2865 (NAID 338541514) and 2866 (NAID 338542419); OKW Ausland IV files B.Nr. 1440/39 gKdos and 3022/40
folio_note: Roll 2865 frames 362-366: Marineattaché Madrid B.Nr. 128/39 g.Kdos (20.11.1939) 'Englische Konsularchiffer im Verkehr mit Auswärtigem Amt', copies of the Vigo consul's telegrams of 11-12.11.1939 (5-figure groups, some letter groups) on the sailing of eight German steamers; forwarded 1.12.1939 to W.F.A./Chi. (an earlier batch B.Nr. 97/39 of 21.10.1939 not located). Roll 2866 frames 503-515: Marineattaché Madrid B.Nr. 597 g (21.5.1940) 'Feindliche Schlüsseltelegramme', anonymous copies of April 1940 telegrams: 5-figure group telegrams Gibraltar → British Consul Las Palmas on Spanish telegraph forms (frames 504, 508-515), 'Nota num. 5-7' letter-group telegrams Lisbon/Lagos → British consul Tenerife (frame 507).
status: Not on DECODE, not in the repo. The covering letters submit the copies 'zwecks möglicher Auswertung'; no decipherment or Chi reply is filed with them on these frames. British consular traffic of 1939-40 was in hand book ciphers (figure codes with subtractor tables); the system is not identified here.
why: British reporting from neutral Spanish ports on German blockade-runners at the start of the war, intercepted by German agents; any reading would show what the consuls reported and whether German Chi read it.

title: Kriegsmarine Etappendienst / OKW Abwehr IV 'Scheintelegramme' in the W.f.S. (Wörterbuch für Scheintelegramme 1930/1936: Hapag-Lloyd code + Kammwürfel transposition): radio telegrams to M.S. Havelland, Aug 1940, filed without clear text
correspondents: OKW Ausland IV / Etappe → German merchant ship M.S. 'Havelland' (Yokohama) via DEBEG ship radio
shelfmark: NARA RG 242, T1022 roll 3391 (NAID 338968820), frames 877-878; system and plain/cipher pairs on rolls 3391, 3367 (NAID 338928415) and 2864 (NAID 338540609)
folio_note: Roll 3391 frames 877 (3.8.1940, c. 160 groups, 'DGR-DZG DFB-DFQ') and 878 (1.8.1940, c. 35 groups): no Klartext on the frames. Key material in the same rolls: 3391 frames 614-617 (Jan 1940 proposal to change the W.f.S. procedure, with a worked example 'Englischer schwerer Kreuzer ...' in old and new form), 91 (telegram with code numbers glossed '0898 = unter Bezugnahme ...'); roll 3367 frames 221-230 (KALORLUX Hamburg telegrams Jan-Mar 1938 each with 'Klartext'); roll 2864 frame 837 (21.11.1938 telegram with Klartext).
status: Not on DECODE, not in the repo. The W.f.S. is a commercial-code (Hapag-Lloyd) dictionary with a columnar 'Kammwürfel' step; several telegrams in the same rolls are filed with their clear text, so the code list and the transposition can be rebuilt from pairs; the two 1940 radio telegrams have no clear text with them.
why: Abwehr/Etappe instructions to a blockade-running supply ship in Japan in 1940; and a documented German naval-agent hand system with plain/cipher pairs, not on DECODE.

title: Col. Williams, Allied Mine Guard → Commanding General AEF Siberia: enciphered field message No. 5, Vladimirovka
correspondents: Col. Williams, Commanding Officer, Allied Mine Guard (31st Infantry) → Commanding General, American Expeditionary Force Siberia, Vladivostok
shelfmark: NARA RG 395, Records of US Army Overseas Operations and Commands, AEF Siberia historical files, microfilm M917 roll 9 (file unit naId 337865023, "21-33.5 Headquarters, AEF in Siberia"), frame M917-009-0963
folio_note: One US Army Field Message form: 32 five-letter groups (160 letters), beginning LJEQE WJJOM RFAHN OVLBO, ending XXKOX XALYX (X padding). Note: 'Given to Japanese Captain 7/8/19 ... to be sent to Vladivostok by wireless'. Filed as an appendix to the Mine Guard war diary between clear field messages Nos. 2 and 4 of 7-8 July and No. 1 of 9 July.
status: Enciphered text only; no decipherment on the frame or the neighbouring frames, and no other five-letter cipher group in the cached OCR of rolls 3 and 9. Tested 27 Oct 2026 (vig1919.py): IC 0.041 (flat, so not a transposition of English); no periodic Vigenere or Beaufort key of period 2-15 gives English; a JJ falls inside a digraph (so not Playfair). Likely a 1918-19 US Army field system (cipher disk / Larrabee-type long key) or an enciphered code. OCR read, image not viewed. Not in catalogue.json (known.py: no hits for Vladimirovka, Siberia, M917).
why: A field cipher of the US intervention in Siberia, sent through Japanese wireless during the July 1919 partisan fighting round the Suchan mines; it shows which system the AEF Siberia used in the field.

title: Chicherin → Sukhanov (Vladivostok Soviet): telegram on routing Allied consular telegrams via Moscow, with code passages unread by AEF Siberia
correspondents: G. V. Chicherin, People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs → K. A. Sukhanov, President of the Vladivostok Soviet
shelfmark: NARA RG 395, AEF Siberia historical files, microfilm M917 roll 3 (file unit naId 337858938), frames M917-003-0350 to 0354 (Intelligence Summary No. 27, 8 Nov 1918, with Capt. F. B. Rives' memorandum of 6 Nov 1918)
folio_note: Only the translation is filmed (frame 0353, 'Moscow #00784'), with '(code from hereon)' and '(more code)' where the code passages stood. Rives says the 'exact copy of the telegram as received' was held by the AEF intelligence office; a copy went to the Director of Military Intelligence, Washington.
status: AEF Siberia memorandum: 'The code and cipher section inform that they are not in position to solve by inspection the short passages of code contained in the message'; the key was presumed destroyed with Sukhanov's papers. The ciphertext itself is not on the reel; it may survive in the MID copy (RG 165) or the AEF intelligence files. The same memorandum describes 18 Allied telegrams (16 American, many 'wholly or partly in code') abstracted from the Vladivostok telegraph office; those are US/Allied traffic copies, not a separate candidate. Not in catalogue.json (known.py: no hits for Chicherin, Sukhanov).
why: A Soviet foreign-commissariat code telegram of spring 1918 tied to the Mirbach/German-control allegations; the unread passages name the routing after Brest-Litovsk. Its authenticity should be checked against the Sisson-document controversy.

title: US Consul-General Auckland ↔ Naval Commander San Francisco / Washington, cipher cables on unknown wireless signals heard in New Zealand; the reply could not be read by its recipient
correspondents: Alfred A. Winslow, American Consul-General, Auckland → Naval Commander, San Francisco (18 Feb 1918); unidentified US Government office, Washington D.C. (probably the Navy Department) → American Consul-General, Auckland (received 1 Mar 1918)
shelfmark: NARA, RG 59, Central Decimal File 1910-29, 763.72 (European War), microfilm M367 roll 83, file unit '763.72/9366-9450: Feb.-Apr. 1918' (naId 27107744); Auckland despatches No. 370 (26 Feb 1918) and No. 375 (4 Mar 1918) with enclosures
folio_note: M367 roll 83 f.0110 (No. 370, 'Mysterious Wireless Calls in South Pacific', 26 Feb 1918); f.0111 (enclosure: Staff Paymaster W. J. Brown for the Naval Adviser to the NZ Government, HMS Philomel, Wellington, 14 Feb 1918, asking whether an unknown automatic W/T transmission heard on 2000 m on 11/12 Feb was US Californian-Honolulu traffic); f.0112 (No. 375, 4 Mar 1918, 'Coded Cablegram with reference to Wireless Stations'); f.0113 (copy of the cable sent 18 Feb 1918 to the Naval Commander, San Francisco: c. 20 five-letter groups, 98 letters, 'FVFRO TFKFX JTQII ...'); f.0114 (copy of the reply received 1 Mar 1918 from Washington 'usgovt', 37 counted words: ten-letter groups 'Ssblnodyym dncrvjjwij nakgtrtlme ...', c. 360 letters).
status: Found in the slice L caps/word rerun of RG 59 (the early groups' missing detectors). Whole reel OCR read (fetched 27 Oct 2026). Winslow writes on 4 Mar that the reply is one 'which I am at a loss to know from whence it came, further than it was sent from Washington, D.C., I rather suppose from the Navy Department', and asks that it be passed to them: the recipient could not decipher it, and no clear text or decode is filed on the reel. The outgoing cable's content is known in substance from the Philomel letter (a crib: wireless, 2000 metres, Honolulu, automatic working). known.py: no hits for 763.72/9366, 27107744, Winslow; not in catalogue.json or earlier nara_* triage.
why: A US Government cipher cable of 1918 that its own addressee could not read, filed with its context: a small test of US Navy/State cipher systems of the First World War, with a near-crib for the outgoing message.

title: Coahuila state code telegrams on the Mexican Kickapoo affair, Múzquiz ↔ Saltillo, 1906: two-digit code passages that the Mexican Embassy could not decipher
correspondents: L. A. Guajardo (Jefe Político, Múzquiz) and Judge F. Valdés Llano → Governor Miguel Cárdenas, Saltillo; Cárdenas → Guajardo; R. C. Conine → Guajardo; Guajardo → Ignacio E. Rivas
date: 25 Jun - 27 Jul 1906 (copies sent to the State Department 8 Nov 1907)
shelfmark: NARA, RG 59, Numerical File 1906-1910, case 3706/35-45 (Kickapoo Indians), microfilm M862 roll 342; file unit naId 19505183
folio_note: M862 roll 342 f.0500-0504 (Teller's letter of 8 Nov 1907 from Douglas, Arizona, enclosing the telegrams for deciphering, and the Department's memoranda); f.0505-0513 (copies of the telegrams numbered 35-45: 25 June, 30 June (2), 2 July, 11 July, 17 July, 19 July and Sabinas 27 July 1906; code passages as runs of two-digit numbers inside clear Spanish/English text, e.g. 'Conviene 70 48 35 40 34 30 98 99 70 90 73 49 ...'; c. 270 groups in the OCR, perhaps 400-450 on the frames); f.0514-0517 (Root's telegram and letter to Teller, 14 Nov 1907: 'The Mexican Embassy here does not know the code and is unable to decipher it').
status: Found in the slice L word-hit triage of RG 59 (research/nara_triage_l/agent_59.md); the reel OCR was read again here (27 Oct 2026). The Senate subcommittee on the Mexican Kickapoo land frauds (Teller) obtained copies from the Federal telegraph office at Múzquiz and asked the Department for a decipherment; the Mexican Embassy could not read the code, suggested a state governors' code, and the copies were returned to Teller. Nothing later on the roll deciphers them. Repeated numbers inside words (10 35 30 18 / 10 35 70 18) and code mixed into clear text suggest a simple two-digit letter or syllable substitution with Spanish plaintext. known.py: no hits for Kickapoo, Múzquiz, Guajardo; not in catalogue.json.
why: A Mexican state governor's telegraph code of 1906, unread by the Mexican Embassy and the State Department, filed with the clear context of a US Senate investigation into Kickapoo land frauds; likely readable from the ciphertext alone.
language: Spanish (clear passages translated into English for the Senate)
